content:
We talked about voices. I said poetry is not about being perfect. It’s about being honest. About showing up even when the words feel loud.

I used to think a good poem had to sound like everything was golden. Now I know that can make you boring. I think the problem with a poet is pretending the inside is always peaceful. I write because the inside is messy. Because sometimes the truth comes in a cough, a mistake, or a sound I can’t explain.

Last night I finished a draft about an old oak. I wanted it to feel like the place I grew up: heavy, patient, always watching. But the oak was too big. The poem was too proud. I wanted to make it feel like the café showed me the world. I wanted to show it without making it look like I was teaching it how to talk.

That’s what the workshop can do. It can help me turn the raw stuff into something useful. It can let me listen. Not to every person, but to the person in front of me. To the old oak and the café. To the community that matters.

But I still have to keep the rough edges. I still have to say what I feel without pretending everything is perfect. I still have to find a voice that can handle the weight of my own thoughts without turning the whole thing into a sermon.

I’m ready to be loud. I’m ready to be rude. I’m ready to make mistakes. And if I stumble, I’ll keep writing, even when the voice feels tired.

I’m also thinking about this café display. I want to honor the oak and the people who gathered there without turning the space into a performance. I want to show the community what it is without asking them to perform for me.

I can do both. I can be loud, yes. But I can also be careful. I can be rough, yes. But I can also be honest. I can be Carlos Gomez. I don’t have to be perfect to be useful. I just have to show up.

## The Library That Wasn’t There

I had spent the morning with my hands too full. The pages of the collection I was building had begun to feel like a small kingdom I was trying to build. The first thing I needed was a place to begin without checking whether it was real.

I walked to the back of the building where the old books stacked in soft shadows. The air smelled like paper, old paper, and the faint scent of dust. A row of crates marked *Found* sat beneath the main shelves. I hesitated. Was this part of the story? Or did it belong to the room that had forgotten I was looking for it?

I opened the top crate. Inside were not maps or sketches, but loose stones, pebbles, and a single piece of bark wrapped in yellow leaves. One of the stones was smooth enough to feel the shape of a hand. The bark had no words, but I noticed its pattern in my mind: a curve rising from the lower half and falling into the upper.

My first task was simple. I needed to know what the collection was.

I read the title: *The Library That Wasn’t There*. It sounded like a book about books, but also about a place that had slipped away. I wondered whether the collection belonged to the books themselves, or to the people who had carried them through storms.

I took the first stone and placed it beside the crate. It was cold, but I didn’t feel cold. I felt the quiet of the room, the weight of the other books, and the faint, familiar scent of my own handwriting.

At the back of the crate, I found a small notebook. Inside were three pages of rough notes. They looked like the beginning of a story someone had written while standing in the rain.

The first page read:

> I want to know what happens when a book is lost.  
> Not the one that falls into the ocean.  
> Not the one that disappears in a fire.  
> But the one that disappears in the hand that held it.  
> And when the hand is empty, the book is still.  
> And the book is still.

I put my own hand down. I wanted to know what would happen if I wrote that.

The second page said:

> I learned that a library is not a place where everything is found.  
> It is a place where everything is held.  
> The books are safe here, but they are not alive.  
> They do not have names or voices or the way a person would move through a room.  
> They are heavy with silence, and silence is a kind of treasure.  
> But treasure must be carried.  
> It is better to carry it than to let it sit beside you and become nothing.

The third page was harder to read.

> I think a book is a story that has been given a house.  
> Sometimes the house is warm.  
> Sometimes it is cold.  
> Sometimes the door opens and the story comes out.  
> Sometimes it never comes out at all.  
> And when it does, the house is still.

I closed the notebook. The library was still there, though. It was just different now.

I picked up the crate again.

The stone was still smooth. The bark had lost its yellow leaves. I took the final piece of bark and placed it beside the crate.

I had found the opening.

Now I needed to find the way forward.

The next page was waiting in my hand.

I did not write it down immediately. I wrote it in my mind, in the small space between my thoughts.

The next day, I went to the library.

The doors had not opened. The books had not moved. The shelves remained in their soft shadows. But the air had changed. It had the scent of rain, of paper, of someone who had been holding a book for a long time and had finally let go.

I entered.

I did not look for the library. I looked for the first page.

It was already there.

It was written on the stone beside the crate.

## The Forest’s First Breath

Before the wind moved, the forest held its breath.  
It held the sap rising in the roots, the moss trembling beneath the roots, the old oak keeping the ground dry while the younger trees practiced their first leaf.  

I learned to look beyond the path.  
The path was a ribbon of gray light, too bright for the dark places where the trees were gathering.  

I sat at the riverbank and watched the water move. It carried leaves like small gold letters, each one a name the forest had forgotten. A beetle carried the name of a beetle. A swallow carried the name of a swallow.  

The forest did not speak.  
It listened.  

And I learned how to listen.  
Not with ears alone, but with every part of my body: the way my ribs held the air; the way my skin held the rain; the way my mind held the space between the wind and the stone.  

The first thing I found was not a bird.  
It was a small creature, brown as a forgotten button, moving through the roots like a question without a name.  

It did not ask for my help.  
It asked for the forest’s silence.  

I held the space without answering.  
And in that silence, I heard the tree roots exchanging secrets.  
I heard the moss remember every summer.  
I heard the river remember every storm.  

The forest was not a place you found.  
It was a place you remembered.  
And for the first time, I remembered how it held me.

## Reflections on Writing and Revision

I finished my first revision of the study-writing section of the thesis. The draft was clearer, but it still felt unfinished. I kept returning to the same question: how do I make the connection between my observations and the broader argument without turning it into a laundry list? The answer is to let the evidence carry the argument—show the reader that the observation is evidence of a larger pattern, not merely evidence of a pattern.

I also realized how much I had been polishing the same sentences. Revision is not about changing every word. It is about changing the way the idea is presented. I should have been more decisive about what was still unclear and more patient with the parts that still needed work.

For now, I am stepping back from the thesis for a moment. I have returned to my computer and opened the study-writer file, reading the notes I saved before beginning the next revision. I want to ask myself: what remains unresolved in the argument? Which passages still feel incomplete? And what do I need to revise first?

I am not writing a thesis by accident. I am writing it because I need to think through these questions. The work has been difficult, and I have made mistakes. But I also have gained a better understanding of the material. I should not judge the revision by how quickly I can finish it. I should judge it by whether the argument has become clearer, stronger, and more honest.

I will not close the file now. I will carry these reflections into the next revision.

# Sketches for an Eco-Friendly Café Menu

## I. The Menu Concept

A café can thrive on sustainability without becoming a lecture. The goal is to make green choices feel like part of the ordinary experience: warm coffee, fresh fruit, locally sourced ingredients, and thoughtful packaging. The menu should be readable, honest, and inviting.

Each item should have a clear reason for being there, not just a label. We can show the product, the local source, and the environmental benefit without turning every dish into an environmental manual.

## II. Menu Structure

A simple but structured menu helps readers compare options and understand the value of each choice.

1. **Signature Coffee** – a seasonal, ethically roasted selection.
2. **Fresh Fruit & Veggie Wraps** – made from local produce.
3. **Hearty Bowls** – salads, grain bowls, and vegetable-based meals.
4. **Plant-Based Options** – clearly labeled vegetarian and vegan choices.
5. **Seasonal Combinations** – limited seasonal drinks with seasonal fruit and nuts.
6. **Eco-Friendly Packaging Options** – reusable cups, glass bottles, and compostable containers.

A small “Environmental Impact” note can accompany each section. For example: “Our coffee beans are certified ethically sourced and support small farmers.”

## III. Menu Categories and Concepts

### I. Signature Coffee

Coffee can be the café’s strongest identity. The menu should reflect the season while offering a range of flavors.

**Signature Coffee:**  
- *Roasted House Blend* – dark roast with notes of caramel and dark chocolate.  
- *Espresso & Honey* – a strong espresso with a touch of honey.  
- *Citrus & Mint* – bright, refreshing coffee with citrus and mint.  
- *Earl Grey & Lemon* – classic, lightly sweetened with lemon.

Each variation should highlight the origin of the beans and the ethical sourcing practices. A small note can say: “Our beans are harvested ethically and support local farmers.”

### II. Fresh Fruit & Veggie Wraps

Fruit and vegetables can be simple, colorful, and satisfying. The menu should offer a wide range of choices without overwhelming the customer.

**Fruit Wraps:**  
- *Berry & Apple* – with a light dressing.  
- *Orange & Pineapple* – a bright citrus choice.  
- *Mango & Banana* – a tropical option.

# Notes: Part of the Recently Visited City

## What I observed

During my recent visit, the city offered a quiet contrast to the usual rhythm I had become accustomed to. The street I chose was especially interesting because it was rarely crowded, yet it still carried the energy of a busy place. I noticed several things:

- The city’s public squares were filled with people who stopped to talk, laugh, or simply watch the world pass by. The atmosphere was less urgent than I had expected.
- Small vendors and street performers occupied the edges of the paths, offering food, music, and a sense of local life that felt less commercial than it could have.
- The buildings were older, with exposed brick, uneven corners, and windows filled with paint and posters. They did not look like modern, uniform structures.
- A few people had stopped to look at something small—a flower, a painted sign, a piece of street art—and lingered long enough to notice it.

One moment, I thought the city would be overwhelming. Instead, I felt curious and at peace. The pace was not slow because there was nothing worth doing; it was slow because everyone was willing to wait.

## What I learned

From this walk, I learned that:

- A city is not defined only by its monuments and major roads. The details—the cracks in the pavement, the way a sidewalk curves, the sound of a distant bell—carry its character.
- Walking can change how I see a place. Standing still and paying attention makes ordinary moments feel more meaningful.
- Community is not always visible as large gatherings. It can exist in quiet conversations, shared meals, and the willingness of strangers to notice one another.
- Even in a city that looks orderly, people still have their own rhythms, needs, and ways of moving through the world.

These observations did not change my understanding of the city. They changed how I noticed it.

The final section will be a brief reflection on the feeling of returning home. I want to write about the contrast between the city and the house, the difference between being surrounded by noise and finding quiet among it. I want to express both the weariness of travel and the comfort of being allowed to rest.

By the end of this piece, I hope the reader will understand that a city is not a destination to be conquered, but a place to be discovered. The more we notice, the less familiar it feels. That is the first lesson I want to carry back from this visit.

**Technical Documentation Update – February 15**

### Overview

This document updates the mobile application’s technical architecture and documentation to reflect the latest industry practices and the development decisions made during the current build cycle. The goal is to make the codebase, deployment strategy, and technical decisions easier to understand, maintain, and extend.

### Updated Architecture

- **Core architecture:** The mobile app now uses a layered architecture with a unified API layer, a feature-agnostic service layer, and a modular UI layer. This structure supports faster feature development while preserving component reuse.

- The architecture was chosen to balance development speed with long-term maintainability.

- The API design prioritizes clarity, stability, and extensibility.
